articles.title_orig: US Futures Rally as Tech Rebound Gains Momentum: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: US Futures Rally as Tech Rebound Gains Momentum: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX shares rose 4.83% in Friday's shortened trading session, amid broader Nasdaq gains and after CEO Elon Musk expanded his SpaceX share-donation plan for U.S. children.
Other tech-related stocks, including Micron , Qualcomm , Lumentum and Tesla all gained over 5% on Friday as the sector rebounded from a heavy sell-off earlier this week. SanDisk was Friday's biggest mover as investors rotated back into some AI trade names , surging 15.96%.
Musk posted on X on Thursday, "I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year."
After Musk's post, SpaceX shares jumped more than 7% in overnight trading on Blue Ocean ATS, an alternative trading system for U.S. equities that runs during the nighttime hours. U.S. stock exchanges were closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and closed at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.
Shares closed 1.30% higher on Wednesday ahead of Thanksgiving.
The latest pledge follows SpaceX's announcement Wednesday that it would donate one share of its Class A stock to all active Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children, with Musk personally matching the gift.
In a separate post on X, Musk said SpaceX's contribution would be transferred next month, while his personal donation would follow when his lockup period expires in June next year.
Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created as of October, according to the White House.
Since the program's launch in July, families and friends have contributed more than $1 billion to the accounts, bringing total deposits from all sources to more than $9 billion, CNBC reported earlier this week.
The FCC also announced Wednesday that it granted SpaceX approval to deploy 1 million data center satellites for the company's Starmind constellation.
Speaking on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Friday, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the authorization of SpaceX's satellites will have ripple effects within the industry as well.
"Not just SpaceX, but all sorts of different players in this market. Because at the end of the day, we want everyone to compete and succeed. I think we're going to see a lot of players entering this space soon," Carr said.

articles.title_zh: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
articles.content_orig:

Russian hybrid attacks could cause a mass-casualty event in Europe, a report has warned, as Moscow steps up sabotage operations across the continent.
The study, carried out by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), found that sabotage operations across the continent had risen by 16 per cent and focused on countries that supported Kyiv.
Poland suffered 24 per cent of all the attacks while Germany faced 20 per cent and the Baltic states – including Latvia , Estonia and Lithuania – faced 20 per cent.
Instances of violent attacks have also increased significantly, with a rise in arson attacks and the use of improvised explosive devices (IEDs).
Russian proxies have demonstrated increased capabilities with more complex IEDs deploying timed and remote detonators.
It comes as Europe has faced cyberattacks across supermarkets, blood banks and airports.
“Sabotage has not yet achieved a strategic effect, but a mass-casualty incident is possible as the space for miscalculation narrows,” the report said.
“A single operation that caused fatalities or prolonged disruption would generate demands for retaliation and likely expose divisions between European governments.”
It predicted that European governments would be likely to continue responding to Russia ’s attacks “one incident at a time”.
“Despite recent attacks and attempted attacks in Estonia, Lithuania and Romania, none has set out red lines, with concern about escalation the primary instinct,” it continued.
It warned: “The effect is that the first mass-casualty attack (deliberate or by miscalculation) would set the terms of Europe’s response, with governments acting under pressure and possibly divided.”
This approach has done little to impact the Kremlin’s strategy and the report offered suggestions on how to improve the chances of changing the Kremlin’s approach.
“Publicly signalling, at least among Nato member states, what level of harm triggers which response would give Europe a better chance of changing the Kremlin’s calculation,” it said.
The study assessed attacks between October 2025 and September 2026.
The fallout from the war has spread beyond Europe too, with a Russian warship sunk in Benghazi, Libya following a Ukrainian attack.
The explosion took place on board Merkury, a Russian navy warship docked at the Benghazi naval base.
Satellite images by Vantor showed the ship was a Russian Navy corvette, or small warship, with pictures showing that most of the vessel had capsized and sunk, with only its bow still visible above water while smoke rises.
It came a day after Finland’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, warned that the Russia-Ukraine conflict was “spilling over” after a Russian ship was reportedly on fire in Finnish waters last Saturday.

articles.title_orig: The man standing up to China in Taiwan’s local elections
articles.title_zh: The man standing up to China in Taiwan’s local elections
articles.content_orig:
Throughout months of campaigning to become the next mayor of Taipei, Puma Shen has been rigorous in his messaging.
He’s focused on urban renewal, boosting business, public transport, jobs for the young and care for the elderly.
He’s trying to win Taiwan’s capital for the Democratic Progressive Party for the first time in more than 30 years. The polls have put him close to - sometimes even in front of - the incumbent he’s trying to unseat.
But the 44-year-old associate professor and lawmaker didn’t make his reputation on local issues.
You’re reading InDepth : A weekly long read from Channel 4 News offering quality analysis and insight, diving deeper beyond the headlines
He’s one of Taiwan’s highest-profile activists on what he sees as the mounting threat from China.
“China, I mean, they might be pissed off,” he tells Channel 4 News. “I mean, I’m the one they’ve already sanctioned, and I might become the mayor of Taipei.”
Shen, pictured below, has been attracting the ire of Beijing for years.
An academic and criminologist, in 2019 he launched Doublethink Lab, to monitor what he calls China’s cognitive warfare on Taiwanese society, in the online space.
Two years later, he co-founded Kuma Academy - to train civilians in civil defence to prepare for a real-world military invasion. Beijing has sanctioned it as a Taiwan-independence organisation, and opened an investigation into Shen on charges of ‘separatism’.
“When I dig into all this information and see how they sanction me, how they denounce me online, I always see it as a study. And I know that the purpose of doing all this, I mean from their side, is to make sure that you feel threatened, you feel scared,” he says.
“So if you have that kind of feeling, you’ve actually lost the battle. So that is why I always detach myself. Even if I am the subject.”
It has recently, though, become more personal.
His campaign team reports suspicious characters at his events. Video shows one man calling someone to say he’s watching Shen, and waiting for his team leader.
Taiwan police have arrested four private investigators on charges they placed a hidden camera in a motorbike parked across the street from Shen’s home.
Shen finds that harder to detach from, saying “I’m a little bit, I guess, maybe angry. Because you know that if you want to target someone, you can target me, but they shouldn’t target my family. My daughter, she’s only six years old. So for me it’s not acceptable.”
“They try to wield this kind of information warfare, legal warfare, try to have transnational repression on me,” he says.
“But every time when they are doing this, they’re actually uniting the Taiwanese people. Because people know that, hey, this is the lifestyle, this is democracy, this is the freedom that we want to keep here in our territory.”
Shen’s opponent is Taipei’s current mayor, Chiang Wan-an ( pictured below).
His roots inside the nationalist party, the Kuomintang, go all the way back to his great grandfather Chiang Kai Shek (via an extra-marital relationship that makes up one branch of the family tree).
Chiang Kai Shek fought and lost the civil war against China’s communists - rebasing his Republic of China to Taiwan in 1949. But in recent decades, the KMT has become the main proponent, in Taiwan, of closer relations with China.
It doesn’t endorse reunification on China’s timeline or terms, just as its rival DPP doesn’t advocate a formal, constitutional claim of Taiwanese independence - but within those parameters, the parties are deeply at odds over China policy.
And all the while, the geopolitics are shifting.
China’s President Xi has made resolving the Taiwan question a key legacy issue. This month has seen the latest set of Chinese military exercises - this time 100 ships deployed, some of them surrounding Taiwan, while a carrier group was stationed to simulate cutting off any US naval deployment.
Then again, President Trump has said he’s “not looking” to travel 9,500 miles to fight a war. He’s delayed a $14bn arms deal for Taiwan , calling it a “negotiating chip” in his talks with China, riding a coach and horses through 40 years of US policy in the process.
Taiwan’s DPP-led government has to weigh that against what have still been strong US arms sales, and a continuing US interest in Taiwan’s stability , as the world’s biggest producer of advanced computer chips.
As much as Shen has tried to focus on the local issues in this local election - aware that many Taipei voters disagree with him on China - he’s also clear he won’t be trimming his views on cross-strait policy.
“China is not a hot topic for the local election,” he says.
“But I think for me, I would never change my attitude or my position on criticising China. Because for me, it’s my responsibility to warn the people here in Taiwan of the risk that we’re facing in the future.”
A rally for Shen in northern Taipei earlier this month drew an estimated 100,000 supporters - representative of a movement they’re calling Ocean Current, after a Chinese character in his written name.
On stage, he played lucky dip with a bottle of supporters’ messages. The one he drew read: ‘Win by a landslide.’ He sank to the floor in mortified laughter.
If he does win on Saturday, there is scant chance of a landslide.
But even a razor-thin victory would represent a big upset in Taipei politics, and send a message across the Taiwan Strait.
The interview included in this story has been edited for clarity and length.
Thanks for reading the latest edition of our InDepth newsletter. Subscribe below to keep up to date with Channel 4 News on Substack.
The civil defence detail is the part that stands out. Shen founding Kuma Academy in 2021 to train civilians, and launching Doublethink Lab in 2019, shows his campaign is built on work that started long before this mayoral race. With the United States holding back a 14 billion dollar arms deal as a negotiating chip, a razor thin victory on Saturday would send a message well beyond Taipei, because it would show voters rewarding that preparation.
I struggle with the media in the West that constantly agitates around the Taiwan issue but seem incapable of addressing the actual countries actively involved in illegal wars. Every aggressive malfeasance by any country is turned into "But China might". Just look at history. In the last fifty years, how many countries has China invaded.
The reality is that Taiwan politics are far more nuanced than this article would have us believe.

articles.title_orig: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.title_zh: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.content_orig:
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."
The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.
On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.
The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.
Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.
"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-François Blanchet told reporters in French.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Blackwell chips found at China data center linked to Alice Huang: Report
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Blackwell chips found at China data center linked to Alice Huang: Report
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Nvidia chips have shown up inside a Chinese data center linked to Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, the onetime paramour of recently reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to a new report.
The Nvidia chips, known as Blackwell semiconductors, turned up inside a Shanghai data center connected to Alice Huang, according to documents reviewed by Bloomberg News .
Until recently, Blackwell semiconductors were among Nvidia’s most powerful processors. President Trump suggested in his recent trip to China that they wouldn’t become available for another “two or three years” for purchase by Beijing.
“In two years or three years, I would, if I were here, I would say, go ahead. You can now sell Blackwells because they’ll have something else,” Trump said during a Fox News interview at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
“As you know, they’re already working on something else that’s going to be superseding the Blackwell chip,” the president said at APEC in Shenzhen, China. “But in two or three years, I’ll say, go do the Blackwells because they’ll be able to do it.”
The Commerce Department approved the sale of tens of thousands of the semiconductors in the last year from US-based Nvidia to countries like the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia — but had banned China from purchasing the Blackwell chips.
Two firms, Yangtze River Delta Project and Shanghai Kezhan, are making use of the chips at the Shanghai data center.
The Yangtze River Delta Project’s president is Kang Wei, the reported husband of Alice Huang.
Huang, the suspected Chinese intelligence asset and affair partner of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang (no relation), is the CEO of Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is currently under investigation by the Commerce Department for evading export controls by allegedly selling chips to China.
In 2024, Megaspeed also used a rendering of Yangtze River Delta Project to show its largest data center to investors — without disclosing the location in China — though it’s unclear if Megaspeed directly diverted the Nvidia chips to that center.
Documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November confirmed that Yangtze River Delta Project received the hardware as collateral for what amounted to a $14 million loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank.
Shanghai Kezhan also got a loan from a Shanghai government agency last year to purchase what turned out to be the Nvidia chips, per lending documents.
Commerce officials first opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, resulting in an attempted interview of Alice Huang in June 2025 — the same month that Nvidia put her company on its “no sell” list.
In its filing earlier this week, Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security said it was blacklisting Megaspeed due to suspicions it was “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.”
It also cited a “significant risk” of Megaspeed “being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.”
Reps for Nvidia and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: UN peacekeepers are preparing to leave southern Lebanon. There’s no plan for what comes next
articles.title_zh: UN peacekeepers are preparing to leave southern Lebanon. There’s no plan for what comes next
articles.content_orig:
By ABBY SEWELL and BASSEM MROUE
BEIRUT (AP) — Lebanon’s prime minister said Friday that a new proposal is in the works that could have the U.N. Security Council allow the peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon to continue working after its nearly 50-year mandate expires at the end of the year.
Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told The Associated Press that the plan would see the peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL continuing its work after Dec. 31 and as the Security Council debates what should replace it.
France is preparing to introduce a resolution, Salam said, which would allow UNIFIL to continue some of its functions — such as clearing mines, escorting humanitarian convoys, and monitoring violations — in southern Lebanon during a drawdown period after the peacekeepers’ mandate ends.
U.S. officials have indicated that Washington is “open to considering” such an arrangement, he said.
“This would not resolve the problem of so-called post-UNIFIL, but it will give us some extra time to agree on a new architecture in southern Lebanon,” Salam said in an exclusive interview with the AP at the government palace in Beirut.
The U.N. Security Council voted last year to terminate UNIFIL’s mandate at the end of 2026, bowing to demands from the United States and its close ally Israel, which argued that the force had failed to stop Hezbollah’s buildup in southern Lebanon.
UNIFIL officials say they were never charged with disarming Hezbollah and that the force helped to preserve calm in the border region for 17 years before Hamas’ 2023 attack on southern Israel ignited a regional war.
The 7,500 peacekeepers currently stationed in southern Lebanon are expected to gradually withdraw over about six months after their mandate expires. The force has a year to fully end its operations.
Much of southern Lebanon, meanwhile, is occupied by Israeli forces after a war broke out in March between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah, linked to the wider Iran war . Hezbollah has refused to give up its weapons, and Israel says it will not withdraw before the group is disarmed.
France has not publicly commented on the proposal that Salam cited.
However, a Western diplomat with knowledge of the matter said one option under discussion is to slow down the withdrawal process and “maintain certain UNIFIL missions” to avoid a power vacuum. The diplomat spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter.
Lebanese officials have called for an extension of UNIFIL’s mandate or, failing that, for a new U.N.-mandated force to be formed.
U.S. officials have expressed willingness for some sort of international force to remain, but not in its current form. They have suggested that it could be a civilian force or private defense contractor.
Salam said that “any force to be deployed will have to be endorsed by the Security Council.”
“I was very clear about it,” he said. Any presence of forces “in the south will have to be endorsed by the Security Council.”
Salam said that with the wider Middle East and especially his region “in flux,” it’s hard to make definitive plans.
Efforts are still underway to form a new government in Israel following last month’s elections, and it remains unclear whether the U.S.-Iran war is heading toward a new escalation or a negotiated solution. Iran is Hezbollah’s main backer.
While the Lebanese government has insisted that its negotiations with Israel are separate from any U.S.-Iran deal, Salam acknowledged that “the relation between the U.S. and Iran directly affects the situation in Lebanon.”
“Lebanon is not an isolated island in the Mediterranean,” he said. “We are very much influenced by developments in the region. The whole region is in turmoil.”
Lebanon and Israel reached an agreement in June under which Israeli forces are supposed to gradually withdraw from Lebanon and hand over control to the Lebanese army, while Hezbollah is to be disarmed.
But implementation has stalled, as have talks between the two countries.
Salam denied that the talks have collapsed but said the “formal negotiations were put on hold” because of the Israeli elections and uncertainty around the composition of the next Israeli government.
It is unclear how an Israeli government potentially headed by opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot instead of current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would differ in its approach to Lebanon, Salam said.
The Lebanese prime minister said that his government has open lines of communication with Hezbollah and Iran but will not “allow the future of the country to be contingent on Iran’s wishes.”
Hezbollah, which has suffered a series of major blows in two recent wars with Israel, seems to be “more and more dependent on Iran” and continues to receive military and financial assistance from Tehran, Salam said.
That’s despite attempts to clamp down on the group’s ability to move money and weapons into the country.
Since the ouster of Syria’s Iran-allied former President Bashar Assad two years ago, the flow of arms from Iran to Lebanon via Syria has slowed but not stopped.
Lebanon remains in a difficult position. Hezbollah has threatened to fight any attempt to forcibly disarm it, and the Lebanese army has so far moved cautiously.
“Definitely we are not seeking confrontation with Hezbollah,” Salam said. “But we will not succumb to the intimidation of Hezbollah.”

If Donald Trump has anything to be thankful for on Thanksgiving, itâs being the âposter boyâ for corruption, Michael Wolff says.
Trump, 80, is spending the holiday weekend in Mar-a-Lago, well aware that Democrats are gearing up for investigations in the new Congress, with the Jensen Huang-Nvidia scandal a priority.
âIf anything at all, one of the things that would reasonably be on his mind...[is] the corruption,â Wolff told Inside Trumpâs Head co-host, Joanna Coles. â[Itâs] the primary thing that the Democrats in Congress are going to focus on: Corruption, his corruption, his familyâs corruption, his sonsâ corruption, his wifeâs corruption, the corruption of his Cabinet secretaries, the corruption of anyone in his orbit.â
If the presidentâs family members, like Don Jr. and Eric, are also there, that does not mean they have the attitude that itâs all for one and one for all, Wolff said.
âI think itâs every man for himself,â he said. âThatâs always been the case among the family. But I think even more so.â
It's "every man for himself" in the face of investigations into Trump and his family, Wolff said.
Wolff said he had spoken to someone who told him there is a new body language in Trumpâs orbit after the midterms.
âEverything has changed. You can pretendâand Donald Trump will pretendâthat it hasnât changed, that he can impose himself at will as he did with Nvidia,â Wolff continued. âBut everything has changed.â
âThe other thing is they donât really know the nature yet of this change,â he continued. âYes, there will be investigations, but what will they feel like? What will they focus on? How scattered will the Democrats be, which might be to their advantage, or how focused they will be, which might... cause a lot of legal bills for a lot of people.â
Photo Illustration by Thomas Levinson/The Daily Beast/Getty/Reuters
Coles added that Democrats could do what Trumpâs people did to them: âforce people to dig into their pocket for real legal advice.â
Democrats have said their investigations into Nvidia and Huang will also involve Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Lutnickâs agency oversees export controls that are aimed at preventing A.I. chips from going to China.
Huang is widely perceived as Trump's point-man on all things artificial intelligence.
Leah Millis/Leah Millis/REUTERS
âCongress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,â House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Monday.
Sens. Chuck Schumer and Elizabeth Warren put out similar messages demanding accountability.

articles.title_orig: Hackers attack and penetrate Air Force’s computing platform
articles.title_zh: Hackers attack and penetrate Air Force’s computing platform
articles.content_orig:
Hackers penetrated the Air Force’s cloud computing platform in a breach that could have exposed sensitive military information, a U.S. official said Friday.
The official confirmed the hack to NBC News but could not  provide any additional information about timing or the attack’s impact.
“The department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems,” an Air Force spokesperson said.
Reuters first reported about this most recent cyberintrusion against federal assets.
The FBI’s National Crime Information Center — which is used by federal, state and local authorities to share important information — was recently breached, sources briefed on the matter told NBC News this week .
And about two months ago, the FBI and Dutch national police arrested leaders of a “global cybercrime and threat actor group” that allegedly stole employee information from a bureau database. It is unclear whether any of these breaches are related.
“We continuously take prudent measures to protect department information, systems, and mission capabilities,” the Air Force spokesperson said Friday. “Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority.”
“The department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet, evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements,” the statement continued. “Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk management processes.”
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Gordon Lubold is a national security reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: By Putin's logic, Russia should be given to Mongolia, Lukashenka says
articles.title_zh: By Putin's logic, Russia should be given to Mongolia, Lukashenka says
articles.content_orig:
Belarusian President Aliaksandr Lukashenka has questioned the logic behind Russia's claims to Ukrainian territory on historical grounds, saying in an interview that following the same reasoning Russia itself should be returned to Mongolia.
Speaking to French magazine Le Point, Lukashenka said that attempts to justify territorial claims by appealing to medieval history were misplaced, citing the period of Mongol domination over the Russian principalities between the 13th and late 15th centuries.
"And today to say that these lands are Russian and have been since time immemorial… At some point they were Russian. But if you look more deeply, Russian lands themselves were once Mongol-Tatar, remember? Then we should hand over the whole of Russia to whom, Mongolia?" Lukashenka said.
He traced East Slavic statehood to the era of Kyivan Rus' in the 11th and 12th centuries — in what is now Ukraine — and said later historical periods could not be used to justify claims on today's independent states.
Lukashenka then appeared to soften the remarks, insisting that Putin "perfectly understands this" and does not dispute the existence of the Ukrainian people or Ukrainian statehood, and that he is simply "misinterpreted".
He added that he shares Moscow's position on "the need for a common future for the peoples of the region."
The remarks echo a 2024 post by former Mongolian president Tsakhiagiin Elbegdorj, who published a "Mongolian historical map" from 1471 on X after Putin gave US conservative journalist Tucker Carlson an extended account of Russian history, showing a diminished Russia within a vast Mongol domain.
"Don't worry. We are a peaceful and free nation," Elbegdorj wrote.
Putin's argument that parts of Ukraine are "primordially Russian" has been central to the Kremlin's official rhetoric since his 2021 article "On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians".
On the eve of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Putin invoked those historical claims explicitly, using them to deny Ukraine's legitimacy as an independent state and to frame the invasion as a correction of a historical injustice.
Historians and international observers have described the Kremlin's attempt to use this precedent as selective and ahistorical.
Lukashenka has ruled Belarus since 1994, making him Europe's longest-serving leader. Following a disputed 2020 presidential election that triggered mass protests and a violent crackdown, he relied on the Kremlin's support to remain in power.
The EU and Western governments did not recognise the election result. Thousands of protesters were arrested, and opposition figures were imprisoned or forced into exile.
Belarus allowed Russia to use its territory to launch parts of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with Russian forces advancing toward Kyiv from the north before being repelled.
Minsk has since remained a close military and political ally of Moscow, although it has stopped short of committing its own troops to the war.
Belarus has faced successive rounds of Western sanctions over both the crackdown on dissent and its role in the war.

articles.title_orig: Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider
articles.title_zh: Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden , moving to Australia.

articles.title_orig: Allstate roiled by tech outage over Thanksgiving week
articles.title_zh: Allstate roiled by tech outage over Thanksgiving week
articles.content_orig:
Allstate has joined the growing list of companies bedeviled by a technology disruption in recent weeks, leaving some customers unable to file claims or seek roadside assistance during Thanksgiving week.
The Northbrook, Illinois-based insurer said in a statement on Wednesday that some of its services had been restricted after customers reported being unable to access them on social media and on Downdetector, which tracks web outages.
"Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims," the company said. "To the extent service interruptions impact a customer's ability to make a payment, they won't lose coverage or be charged late fees."
People seeking roadside assistance on Allstate's website encountered an error message through Friday.
In a statement on its website, Allstate added that customers may reach the insurer through multiple channels, including by phone.
Allstate offers a range of policies, including home, life and auto insurance. Its consumer-facing tech problems during one of the busiest times of year for road travel follow disruptions at other major U.S. airlines, banks , software providers and government agencies.
Microsoft, which suffered a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, said a technical issue caused the disruption and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio also said at the time that the tech outages were distinct from one another. The incidents were caused by companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading outdated systems, they said.
"In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago," Rubio said. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind."

articles.title_orig: Are tech founders and CEOs 'too big to fail?' Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return sparks debate
articles.title_zh: Are tech founders and CEOs 'too big to fail?' Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return sparks debate
articles.content_orig:
'The Big Money Show' panel analyzes Nvidia market volatility, bipartisan backlash over China ties and the broader outlook for semiconductor stocks, Tesla and SpaceX.
The return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO less than two weeks after his resignation is raising questions over whether co-founders and leaders of major tech companies are being viewed as "too big to fail."
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, stepped down as chief executive on Nov. 12 after reports emerged about his extramarital affairs. While the board said during a Nov. 17 earnings call that it wasn't planning to reinstate him, it ultimately reversed course on Nov. 23.
The Huang case at Nvidia follows the saga of OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman, who was ousted as CEO by the AI giant's board following a 2023 power struggle in which he was accused of not being candid with the board. Altman was reinstated within a week after many of the ChatGPT-maker's employees threatened to quit.
Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s ascent to becoming one of the world’s most valuable companies has highlighted "key-man risk" – a firm’s reliance on a single leader for critical operational and strategic decisions.
WHAT JENSEN HUANG'S RETURN MEANS FOR NVIDIA – AND WALL STREET
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was reinstated this week after he resigned earlier this month. (Lisi Niesner/Reuters)
Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, told FOX Business that "Jensen and the other major tech CEOs are the linchpin to the AI Revolution and the global economy. It's key-man risk front and center in this tech world and that is not changing. Jensen is not replaceable."
Gil Luria, managing director at D.A. Davidson, said that the Nvidia situation is "highly unusual" as it's the most profitable company in the world, telling FOX Business that "Mr. Huang's role went beyond CEO of a single company, and the impact of his departure was evident in last week's stock market declines."
Stephen Henriques, a senior fellow at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute, told FOX Business that "as with any company or industry, nothing should be too big to fail," and noted that companies including Apple , Google parent Alphabet, Microsoft and Uber have all seen success after the departure of founding leaders.
"These are obviously great, formidable founders – but the idea that they're too big or too important to fail is honestly, I think, untrue," he added.
NVIDIA REINSTATES JENSEN HUANG AS CEO EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWING US GOVERNMENT INPUT
President Donald Trump called for Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang before they did so. (Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images)
Henriques said that the organizational structure at Nvidia, which reportedly had Huang overseeing 60 direct reports, was too unwieldy and underscored the lack of proper succession planning . He said that in a "normal, well-functioning governing structure, you're going to have a planned successor ready to go in that case Jensen has a heart attack or is hit by a bus, God forbid."
"Most trillion-dollar companies, especially, should have these succession plans ready to go and a clear successor," Henriques said.
He added that most CEOs normally have three or four direct reports who oversee their own business lines and "keep the CEO up to speed and running and allow him or her to have the ability to do what Jensen does … being the face of the organization and the strategic executor."
TRUMP DOUBLES DOWN ON CALL FOR NVIDIA TO REHIRE JENSEN HUANG AMID ALLEGED CHINESE SPY SCANDAL
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was ousted from his role in 2023 amid a power struggle with the AI giant's board, but was reinstated amid employee backlash. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Patrick Moorhead, CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy, told FOX Business that succession planning is "essential" and that it's "where Nvidia's board quite frankly failed: it still owes investors a succession plan."
"With roughly 60 direct reports and command and control running through one person, nobody steps into Jensen's chair as is, so a real plan is a visible bench of leaders who already make big decisions, the way Apple had Tim Cook running operations for years before Steve Jobs handed over the job," he said.
Moorhead said that he is "not one to call for more regulation, but every tech board should have a director accountable for signing off on a succession plan, including at companies where the founder holds voting control. Key-man risk doesn't go away when the founder comes back; it just goes back into hiding."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"A founder's value is in the next bet, not the next quarter. Nvidia's supply and roadmap are locked, so the business never needed saving for 2027. But Jensen has bet the company on new platforms and been right, and his return restores the next round of big bets and keeps the talent that stayed for him," Moorhead explained.
"OpenAI showed the same pull in 2023, when nearly all of its staff threatened to walk and Sam Altman was back within a week," he added.

articles.title_orig: America's new bargain hunt
articles.title_zh: America's new bargain hunt
articles.content_orig:
Cash-strapped consumers are changing they way they spend money. As essentials like rent and utility bills gobble up more of their budget, some families are dialing back on groceries or eating out.
When the cost of renting, gasoline and heat goes up, something's got to give. Many families are cutting corners at the grocery store in order to pay their other bills. NPR's Scott Horsley reports on new findings from a credit union that followed millions of families through the spending squeeze.
SCOTT HORSLEY, BYLINE: Jody Levin just got an eye-popping bill for heating oil. At $6.49 a gallon, just staying warm this winter is going to cost Levin and her husband more than $800 a month.
JODY LEVIN: It's very, very stressful. It's hard on our marriage. It's hard on our budget. They have tripled in costs since we've lived here.
HORSLEY: Levin lives about an hour outside Seattle and works in sales. Her husband works for a company that makes computer parts. They've cut back on concerts and restaurant meals and are watching their pennies at the supermarket.
LEVIN: We don't have meat as much, I think more pasta than usual, or, like, a baked potato, broccoli and cheddar, you know, like, just cutting back on big-ticket items like fish.
HORSLEY: Robin McMillan, who recently retired to Glendale, Arizona, is feeling a similar pinch. While gas prices have come down from their wartime peak, they're still about 18% higher than they were this time last year.
ROBIN MCMILLAN: Gasoline is outrageous. Automobile insurance is just about unaffordable. Groceries are through the proverbial roof.
HORSLEY: McMillan hunts for markdowns on fresh food that's nearing its expiration date. And she's more likely now to choose cheaper store brand products.
MCMILLAN: I used to be a brand snob, but when I saw the reality of my monthly budget, I go, no, I can't do this. We just - we can't afford this.
HORSLEY: A new study from the Navy Federal Credit Union finds cost-cutting at the grocery store is increasingly common. The credit union has been tracking the spending habits of 6 million members across the country for the last two years. Chief economist Heather Long says many are scrimping on food bills as they try to offset the rising cost of housing, energy and insurance.
HEATHER LONG: There's a lot of strain right now. It's a squeeze for many households. And part of the frustration that you see with this economy is not only are - prices are high, but people are not able to spend and shop in the way that they were even two years ago.
HORSLEY: Spending was propped up a bit in the spring and summer by tax refunds, which were 10% bigger on average this year than last. But by September, Long says that cushion was gone. Now, even upper-income families are dialing back their spending on food.
LONG: There's a reason that pick-another-protein ad really resonated in Mississippi. But really, across America is clearly - we can see it in our data. Every single income level has tried to scale back on their grocery spending.
HORSLEY: Erin King lives in Starkville, Mississippi. She reluctantly did pick another protein, even though she says ground turkey is not the same.
ERIN KING: The price of beef is absolutely insane, so we just don't eat beef really anymore.
HORSLEY: King's husband works for a grocery store. She works as a school counselor and earns some extra money working at her church. Despite downsizing to a smaller apartment, she says it's not easy for the couple to make ends meet.
KING: We're still living paycheck to paycheck. We're not really able to save for anything. Like our sofas - it's in rough shape. We can't afford to buy a house. We can't save for that.
HORSLEY: Retailers are expecting a healthy jump in holiday spending this year, but much of that will come from upper-income households. For middle- and lower-income families, any splurge around Christmas will likely mean further belt tightening in the new year.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.

articles.title_orig: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
articles.title_zh: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
articles.content_orig:
Cybersecurity threats escalate as Leah Siskind analyzes Google’s warning about hackers using AI to automate cyberattacks against companies. Discussing the battle between defenders and attackers with John Roberts, the FDD AI Research fellow references Anthropic’s release of advanced models months ago. Siskin warns that super advanced AI models now have the dangerous ‘ability to detect vulnerabilities’ in software systems.
Think about everything sitting in your Gmail inbox right now. Maybe there's a conversation with your doctor, a recent bank statement or a personal message you never intended anyone else to read. Your Google Drive may hold years of private documents. You probably don't spend much time thinking about who might see that information beyond the people you share it with. But what happens when you connect those services to Google's Gemini AI assistant ?
An independent researcher has raised concerns about how Gemini handles information retrieved from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The findings prompted questions about whether some private content could end up in conversations reviewed by humans.
We contacted Google, and the company confirmed that some information retrieved from connected Gmail and Drive accounts may be seen by human reviewers under certain circumstances. Google stressed that these connections are off by default. Here's what you should know before giving Gemini access to your personal information.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
Google's Gemini assistant can retrieve information from connected Gmail accounts to answer questions, raising concerns about how private emails may be handled. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
An independent researcher using the name thisisme6598 published findings on GitHub, raising questions about the way Gemini retrieves information from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts . The researcher tested Gemini using a personal Google Account with connected apps enabled. According to the published findings, Gemini sometimes retrieved information from emails or files during conversations without someone explicitly asking it to search Gmail or Drive. For example, the researcher described asking Gemini whether an internet service bill seemed too expensive. During some tests, Gemini reportedly retrieved billing information from Gmail, including payment amounts, account details and confirmation numbers.
In certain instances, the researcher reported that Gemini returned several sentences directly from an email and, in some tests, the entire email, including its headers. The researcher argues that this behavior creates a privacy concern because information retrieved into a Gemini conversation may become eligible for human review. However, the published findings do not establish that a human reviewer actually accessed the researcher's emails. Google told CyberGuy that the reported retrieval was standard behavior for someone who had voluntarily connected their apps. The company also emphasized that retrieved files remain visible only to the authenticated account holder and are not exposed publicly through this process.
Yes, under certain circumstances. Google's own Connected Apps privacy documentation confirms that trained human reviewers, including service providers, may review a subset of information processed through Gemini's connected apps. That information can include summaries or excerpts from relevant Gmail messages and Google Drive documents.
In some cases, Google acknowledges that reviewers may see a complete email or file if it is short or especially relevant to the request. Google also says human reviewers may access some Gmail inbox content when investigating abuse or harm or responding to submitted feedback.
The company uses these reviews to evaluate Gemini's responses and improve its services.
Simply using Gmail or Google Drive does not subject your private content to this review process. The concern involves information retrieved after someone voluntarily connects those services to consumer Gemini. Google says it does not train generative AI models directly on someone's entire Gmail inbox or Drive. However, relevant information processed during Gemini conversations may be used for model improvement, depending on account settings. Google specifically warns against connecting apps containing confidential information someone would be uncomfortable having a reviewer see.
We contacted Google directly to ask whether human reviewers could access Gmail messages or Drive files processed through the consumer Gemini app. We also asked whether the company had changed its privacy disclosures, notified existing customers and provided ways to prevent human review. A Google spokesperson told CyberGuy:
"Gmail and Google Drive’s core privacy protections remain unchanged, and your private emails and files are not reviewed by humans simply by using Gmail, Drive, or built-in Workspace features. Connecting those apps to the consumer Gemini app is off by default — it’s an optional way to get more personalized, time-saving answers across your Google apps when you want them. Users can disconnect their apps in Gemini settings at any time without losing access to Gemini’s core features."
Google also confirmed that when someone connects their apps to consumer Gemini with activity saving enabled, a small subset of conversations may undergo human review. Those conversations can contain relevant information retrieved from connected services. Before trained service providers review the material, Google says it separates the conversations from the associated Google Account and takes steps to reduce identifying information. The company also disputes the suggestion that the researcher's findings demonstrate public exposure of private files.
Another part of the controversy involves changes to Google's public privacy disclosures . In Oct. 2023, Google published a blog post about its approach to generative AI privacy. The company said that content from Gmail, Docs and Drive accessed through Bard's Workspace extensions would not be seen by human reviewers or used to train the Bard model.
On Oct. 16, 2026, Google added an update to that same blog post. The new language explains that Google has introduced additional optional features allowing people to connect Workspace information to other Google services. Google says that when someone enables these newer features, a subset of the information may be used to train generative AI models, depending on their settings. It may also undergo human review in limited circumstances. The researcher argues that the change represents a reversal of Google's earlier privacy commitment.
However, Google's original statement concerned Bard's Workspace extensions, while the updated disclosure addresses newer connected features. The available evidence does not establish that Google quietly changed the underlying handling of information in existing connections. articles.title_orig: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
articles.title_zh: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
articles.content_orig:
Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.
The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases . Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

articles.title_orig: Airline Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
articles.title_zh: Airline Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
articles.content_orig:
Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year.
Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations.
"Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday.
It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further.
"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution," Norse Atlantic CEO Eivind Roald said.
"We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald added.
The company has canceled all flights, and ticket sales have been discontinued.
Norse was founded in March 2021 and offered cheap flights between Europe, North America, Africa and Asia.
The Iran war began on Feb. 28 and caused jet fuel prices to skyrocket, forcing airlines around the world to grapple with higher costs. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor .
Norse Atlantic's Roald told CNBC in May that he wasn't "overly concerned" about access to fuel but flagged that the company had canceled over 700 flights, which impacted more than 240,000 passengers.
Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary warned in April that if jet fuel prices continued to stay elevated throughout the year, then other European airlines were likely to face "financial difficulties" during the winter season.
In fact, several European airlines have stopped operating this winter, including Slovakia's AirExplore, Spain's AlbaStar, Ireland's Fly4 and Spain's Plus Ultra, which has canceled all flights but hasn't permanently closed.

articles.title_orig: All safe codes in GTA 6 and where to find them
articles.title_zh: All safe codes in GTA 6 and where to find them
articles.content_orig:
Regardless of whether you're exploring criminal compounds or strange research outposts in GTA 6 , you'll frequently come across locked safes full of cash , valuables and illegal goods to fence off . Annoyingly, the residents of Vice City are damn good at keeping their valuables secure, and these safes are tricky to get into unless you use explosives, which bring unwanted attention.
To counter that, you'll need to find safe codes , which you'll discover by exploring. They're well worth the effort though, as they let you crack open safes without making a sound. Below, we've covered where to find all the safe codes in GTA 6 , so you can bypass every safe door and loot all the valuables inside.
Below, we've listed every safe in GTA 6 and the code required to open it. If you want to know how to find the codes for these safes, we've gone into more detail further down the page. Click each safe you want a more detailed explanation for, and you'll skip right there.
Here's every safe and safe code in GTA 6 :
This page is a work in progress. More safes and solutions coming soon!
The safe is found while completing the Kingpin Bowling alley Illegal Operation in Port Gellhorn. Track down the storage room , and look in the office adjacent to it . You'll find the safe in the back left-hand corner.
Found while completing the Brooks and Boatworks Illegal Operation in Port Gellhorn. You'll find an office on the right-hand side of the compound , near the boat in front of the warehouse. On the wall inside is a map , with multiple safe codes printed on it. The Kingpin Bowling Alley code is included.
The safe is found while completing the Brooks and Boatworks Illegal Operation in Port Gellhorn. It's located in the room up the stairs to your left when entering the front doors of the Brooks and Boatworks warehouse. It's to the left of the pool table, near a white plastic chair.
Found while completing the Brooks and Boatworks Illegal Operation in Port Gellhorn. You'll find an office on the right-hand side of the compound , near the boat in front of the warehouse. On the wall inside is a map , with multiple safe codes printed on it. The Brooks and Boatworks safe code is included.
The safe is found while completing the La Cascara Illegal Operation in Port Gellhorn. It's locked in a small cell in the centre of the motel's top floor .
Found while completing the Brooks and Boatworks Illegal Operation in Port Gellhorn. You'll find an office on the right-hand side of the compound , near the boat in front of the warehouse. On the wall inside is a map , with multiple safe codes printed on it. The La Cascara Motel safe code is included.
Found in the Pelican Valley Outpost in Pelican Valley. Upon entering the house in the centre of the outpost, you'll find the safe directly to your left.
While exploring the house in the centre of the Pelican Valley Outpost, view the engravings in the floor in the bedroom. You'll see that " CLEAVES " is scratched into the floor. Once you've viewed it, head to the computer in the living room and choose CLEAVES when asked for a password. It'll reveal a clue, claiming that the code is " double success ."
After a nasty surprise upon exiting the PC screen, head to the shed near the main house, and you'll find a smashed crab tank inside. Near the tank is a list of crab statistics. One of the crabs in the list is highlighted, with a note claiming 00.36 was a "success" . Double 00.36 and you'll have your code.
Found in the Nova Auto Junkyard as part of an Illegal Operation in Hamlet . Head to the bottom of the junkyard and break into the garage near the broken-down school bus. Inside, you'll spot the safe in a storage room.
In the same garage as the safe, you'll find the '77 Albany Teniente Manana low rider , which counts as valuable. Read the number plate, and you'll get the safe code.
Found in Delights Cabaret in Port Gellhorn. You can't access the safe until you complete the story mission " Afternoon Delight ," at which point you'll be guided to the safe in the back of the club.
As the mission begins, Jason and Lucia will receive a text from Vicki, revealing the safe code.
Found while completing the Farm Fix Meth Lab Illegal Operation in Belville . Enter the main drug lab in Farm Fix, then cross the second-floor catwalk to reach an office. The safe is located inside this office.
The code is found in the back room of Farm Fix's main drug lab. When entering the room, you'll see some glowing cabinets, and to the right of them, a small workbench. You'll find a notepad on top of this workbench with the safe code.
Found while completing the Saber Shipping Facility Illegal Operation in Vice City's Salton district . In the main shipping building, look for an office on the second floor. You'll find the safe in the corner.
The code for the safe is found in the same office as the safe . Look for a map on the wall, directly opposite where you entered the office . On this map, you'll see three codes. Jason or Lucia will automatically memorise the code, but it's the top code labelled on the map.
Found while completing the Casa Guardia Illegal Operation in Vice City's Little Cuba district . Head to the second-floor landing of Casa Guardia , and you'll find the safe behind a desk, above the entrance to the building.
The code for the safe is found while completing the Saber Shipping Facility Illegal Operation in Vice City's Salton district . Head to the second floor of the Shipping Facility and look for an office. Directly opposite where you enter the office, you'll see a map on the wall .
On this map, you'll see three codes. Jason or Lucia will automatically memorise the code, but it's the middle code on the map.
Found while completing the Saber Shipping Yard Illegal Operation in Vice City's Little Cuba district . When raiding the main shipping yard building, look for an office at the back of the building. Beside the desk, you'll find the safe.
The code for the safe is found while completing the Saber Shipping Facility Illegal Operation in Vice City's Salton district . Head to the second floor of the Shipping Facility and look for an office. Directly opposite where you enter the office, you'll see a map on the wall .
On this map, you'll find three codes. Jason or Lucia will automatically memorise the code, but it's the bottom code on the map.
Found while completing the Janjak's Garage Illegal Operation in Vice City's La Perle district. You'll find it in the shop, directly to your left when entering through the front gate. Track down the office area of the shop, and you'll find the safe.
After finding the safe, look in the kitchen to your left. On the fridge, you'll spot a post-it note, which you can read to find the safe code.
Found in the back of Victoria Lee Jeweler in Capri's town centre . When holding up the shop, you can find the safe in the back rooms , next to the store's kitchen counters.
When heading through the staff door on the shop floor, enter the first door on your left. Inside the office it leads to, you'll find a post-it note with the code for the safe beside a laptop.
Found in the back of Richardson Jewelry & Diamonds in Vice City's Downtown district . After entering the back door, you'll find it on your right. The safe is mandatory, as you'll have to open it as part of Yasmani's Jewelry Jobs.
You'll automatically get this safe code as part of the Yasmani's Jewelry Jobs mission chain.

articles.title_orig: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington
articles.title_zh: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington
articles.content_orig:
Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday for a snap election that could bring down socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has repeatedly clashed with U.S. President Donald Trump.
It could also put the far right in government for the first time in the country's modern democratic era.
The center-right Popular Party is the frontrunner, and it could win a majority with far-right Vox, according to El País ' s final polling averages . A government led by the PP could shift Spain's approach to Washington, Beijing and NATO.
It's the first test of whether Europe's mainstream conservatives are willing to bring the far right into government, ahead of elections in France and Poland next year.
Despite Spain's economy growing 2.7% year over year in the third quarter, more than twice the euro zone's 1.3%, the campaign has been dominated by housing and cost-of-living crises.
Inflation soared to 4.9% in the year to October, above a euro zone average of 4%. November's flash estimate published Friday showed Spanish inflation cooling to 4.1%, still well above the 2.3% reading at the start of the year. In an October YouGov survey, 53% of respondents named housing one of the country's two most important issues.
Home purchase prices nearly doubled in the decade to the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat . In 2025, house prices rose nearly three times as fast as household incomes, the European Commission said.
Nationwide protests began after an 87-year-old woman died two weeks after being evicted from her Madrid apartment in September.
Sánchez called the snap election after lawmakers rejected two government decrees designed to broaden housing protections, including limiting rent increases and blocking certain evictions and automatic lease renewals. Congress later ratified a revised version of one decree, limiting rent increases and evictions in some circumstances.
Sánchez has made a name for himself internationally after clashing with Trump over NATO spending, the war in Gaza and Spain's refusal to let U.S. forces use its bases for operations against Iran. Trump even threatened to cut off "all trade" with Spain during the dispute over the bases.
At a Nov. 21 rally in Tenerife, Sánchez asked: "What good has President Trump brought to the United States and, by extension, to the world?"
He has also told voters that the PP and Vox would roll back government cost-of-living assistance. Days before the election, Sánchez's government approved 1.21 billion euros ($1.33 billion) to extend public transport discounts through 2027 and approved a general pay increase of up to 4.5% for 2027.
But in a final pre-election survey for El Español on Nov. 23, 66% of respondents gave Sánchez a failing grade and 29.5% a passing one. His government has faced scrutiny over its handling of the Ceuta migrant crisis, two deadly train collisions this year and corruption cases involving people close to the prime minister.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the current favorite to replace Sánchez, has made alleged government corruption and inflation central to his campaign. At a Nov. 22 rally in Murcia, he said the government wanted voters to forget "that inflation is eating into your pay check, that you can't afford a home, that you're paying more than ever for everything."
The PP led the final El País polling average, published Nov. 24, with 31.4%, followed by Sánchez's Socialists at 29.1% and Vox at 17.9%. Several seat projections put the PP and Vox above the 176 seats needed for a majority in the 350-seat lower house. If Vox joins a government, it would be the first far-right party to do so since Spain returned to democracy after Francisco Franco, the dictator who ruled for 40 years, died in 1975.
The PP wants to repeal the 2023 housing law and scrap rent caps in designated high-pressure areas. It proposes speeding up construction permits and lowering taxes on first homes for buyers under 40. Vox also wants to repeal the housing law and would prioritize Spanish citizens for subsidized housing and public services.
Sánchez's Socialists want to extend renter protections and make at least a quarter of new homes public or permanently price-restricted. It would use proceeds from a bank levy to support housing, which it says will raise a further $1.5 billion. The PP has pledged to scrap this.
The PP also favors easing climate rules, extending the life of nuclear plants and replacing a decree that sets tight new renewable-power requirements on data centers with large new grid connections.
A PP-Vox coalition would have its tensions, with immigration likely to be a major pressure point as Vox has an increasingly hard line on deportation and the militarization of some borders. The parties clashed in regional governments over the distribution of unaccompanied migrant children, leading Vox to quit several coalitions in 2024.
Immigration has since gained more prominence amid the government's handling of reports that more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on July 30 and 31.
"Immigration has played a significant role in supporting Spain's recent growth, a strong role for Vox could complicate the government's ability to sustain that," said Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
The parties also differ on defense commitments: both support more investment, but neither has committed to NATO's target of spending 5% of GDP on defense. The PP pledges closer NATO cooperation, while Vox puts greater emphasis on border security.
The PP favors closer integration with the European Union, while Vox wants more independence from it. The success or failure of a PP-Vox partnership will also have wider lessons for Europe "where long-standing firewalls against far-right parties are coming under strain," added Middleton, pointing to the rise of Germany's AfD and the prospect of Marine Le Pen potentially winning next year's election in France.
A shift to the right could improve relations between the U.S. and Spain. Sánchez used his tenure to strengthen ties with Beijing, the country's largest goods trading partner outside the EU.
The U.S. remained Spain's largest source of foreign direct investment. Flows more than doubled to 11.6 billion euros in the 12 months through June 2026, from 5.1 billion euros in the previous 12 months, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Carla Hobbs, head of the European Council on Foreign Relations' Madrid office, expects a PP-led government to seek closer ties with Washington and bring its China policy more in line with the EU's. Vox could complicate that. The first test for Washington would be whether a new government changes Spain's position on defense spending or the use of its bases.
